articles.title: US trade gap in July hits biggest in a year
articles.text: Washington: The US trade deficit in July widened to its largest since March 2025, government data showed Thursday, as imports climbed on the back of the booming AI tech build-out.US trade has seen wide fluctuations since President Donald Trump returned to the White House last year and rolled out sweeping tariffs on allies and competitors, in efforts to narrow the trade gap.But the trade deficit in the world's biggest economy grew to $88.6 billion in July -- a 24.4 percent increase from the month prior -- as exports of crude oil and gold fell while imports of tech products jumped.Read more: US manufacturing growth cools in August as input prices stay highExports dipped 2.1 percent to $310.7 billion, the Department of Commerce said.Imports rose 2.8 percent to $399.3 billion, bolstered by computers, computer accessories and semiconductors.The US deficit with Taiwan, a major manufacturer of chips, reached a record $20.7 billion for the month.US trade gaps with Mexico, Thailand, South Korea and Malaysia for the month also hit their highest on record.While Trump's tariffs have hit economies representing the majority of US trade, American officials have been careful to exempt products like chips, smartphones and other types of electronics.Read more: India wants tariff edge before signing final US trade deal: Piyush GoyalWashington is looking to develop new tariffs on semiconductors, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick told CNBC Wednesday, although adding that tech giants are aware of the Trump administration's plans."What you're going to see is targeted, thoughtful tariff policy that basically says if you build here, you don't pay," Lutnick said.Over the past year, businesses have scrambled to step up imports before new waves of US duties kicked in.Although the US Supreme Court struck down many of Trump's global tariffs in February, officials in July replaced them with fresh duties targeting 60 trading partners.A separate trade investigation taking aim at 16 partners including China, the European Union and Taiwan, could lead to a further round of tariffs.The United States meanwhile is engaged in a trade war with neighboring Canada, with which its deficit narrowed in July. Last month, Trump slapped a 50-percent duty on billions of dollars in Canadian goods, prompting Ottawa's planned retaliation.Also weighing on trade flows is fallout from the Middle East war, with Iran largely blocking off the Strait of Hormuz -- a key waterway for global energy and fertilizer transit.This has helped to raise demand for US energy products but US firms have been grappling with snarled supply chains.

articles.title: Haiku OS rises / Beta 6 sails open web / Virtual winds fly fast
articles.text: The sixth beta of the Haiku OS is here, now with more choice of web browsers and a working hardware-accelerated hypervisor. Haiku OS beta 6 came out just a week after the project’s 25th birthday. We have been trying it on several different machines around the Irish Sea wing of Vulture Towers, and enjoying the experience very much. The release notes contain a lot of changes and some significant new features, although many of them are not immediately obvious. The built-in WebPositive browser is now based on the WebKit rendering engine, which means it handles even demanding web apps such as Gmail perfectly. On Windows and Linux, Google’s Blink dominates, but its ancestor WebKit is a major browser engine in its own right, with first-class support in almost all web apps – mainly thanks to a billion or so Apple iDevices. If you want a big-name browser, though, there is a complete port of Firefox, with official Mozilla branding. What’s more, the project isn’t sticking to the slower-moving ESR version – since we installed beta 6, Firefox has been updated to the latest Firefox 155. You can also choose other Mozilla-family browsers, such as Waterfox, LibreWolf, or Floorp. GNOME Web is still there as well, but now that WebPositive is so capable there’s less need for it. We did notice a flickering mouse pointer with a square outline around it in Firefox, but this is just a cosmetic glitch. While we’re on Mozilla tools, there’s also IceDove, which is Thunderbird 153 ESR without Mozilla branding (and its browser companion IceWeasel, plus IceWeasel ESR). There are plenty of other email clients to choose from, including Balsa, Claws, and the terminal-based Mutt. The other change that could make this a more viable option is significantly faster virtualization. Haiku B6 now has hardware-accelerated VMs, thanks to a port of the NVMM hypervisor. Although NVMM was originally written for NetBSD, it’s not specific to that OS: first it was ported to Dragonfly BSD, and now Haiku thanks to a GSoC project. NVMM makes it possible to start QEMU VMs using the native virtualization features of Intel and AMD CPUs. Both NVMM and Firefox (and relatives) are only available on the x86-64 version of Haiku. The same Beta 6 release is also available for 32-bit x86, and while this doesn’t have some of the new features, it does boast binary compatibility with the original BeOS. Haiku isn’t completely tied to the Intel architecture, though: there are at least three active RISC ports – one for RISC-V 64, one for Arm64, and the experimental PowerPC version. The latter is the oldest, in part being a return to the roots of Haiku’s direct ancestor BeOS – whose original native hardware was the dual-PowerPC BeBox. Although there has been recent progress on the Arm64 and PowerPC versions, this is in part thanks to the use of AI coding assistants. As a result, they are unlikely to be merged back upstream. Sadly, one of the developers working on the Arm64 version halted all their efforts because the Haiku project would not accept AI-generated contributions. The other is now called Tabby-PPC by Sean Malseed, better known on YouTube as ActionRetro. Malseed seems happier to remain an independent fork. Haiku’s AI-free stance is emphasized by the default search engine in WebPositive – https://noai.duckduckgo.com/. Beta 6 has been tightened up in multiple places: it’s a bit smaller, significantly faster in some places, and should use a little less memory than before. Given that it was already quite small and fast, this is impressive. In our testing, it worked well on a UEFI-based Thinkpad X220 with a Core i5, and on an older BIOS-based Thinkpad X200 with a Core 2 Duo. It runs well in 8 GB of RAM, and should be perfectly usable in less. It’s an excellent candidate if you have a very old, low-end PC lying around that you’d like to revive. We have seen comments from some fans of FOSS Unix-like OSes who don’t see the appeal – for instance, we’ve seen multiple comments that it lacks containers. This is true, it does, but this is a graphical desktop OS for a single-user machine. There isn’t even a login screen, and user accounts are purely cosmetic. It’s your computer, and you are the administrator at all time. Haiku is not attempting to be a server OS – there are plenty of those if that’s what you want. What’s more, servers constitute a role for which Linux and the BSDs are very well suited. The hardcore Unix folks may never understand, much like Xkcd’s tech support line. Haiku is not a Linux distribution, nor is it a BSD. It is its own thing, implemented from the bare metal upwards, mostly in C++. It doesn’t use X11 or Wayland. It has a pretty good app catalog these days – and because it has strong POSIX compatibility, many of those apps are Linux ports. That’s no bad thing: it fixes one of the key problems BeOS had. There are native versions of Firefox, LibreOffice, VLC, and so on in the repositories. There are clients for Discord, Matrix, and more, plus Chat-o-Matic, a libpurple-based multiprotocol chat client that can use Pidgin connectors. There are quite a few games and emulators. The HaikuDepot app is a friendly GUI front-end to the software repository, with automatic dependency resolution. It’s also the software updater. If you are interested in a different flavor of Unix, this is probably not the OS you’re looking for. On the other hand, if you want something fast, lightweight, which supports quite a lot of commodity hardware and runs well on old, low-end machines that would struggle to run any modern Linux, then take a look. We love its 1990s-style subtly 3D-shaded GUI, which we find a delightful and refreshing change from the flat translucent look of most modern GUIs. Haiku is a recreation of BeOS, and Be was founded by former Apple exec Jean-Louis Gassée, so there’s a strong Classic MacOS feel to the GUI. (Haiku doesn’t have much resemblance to modern macOS – as in OS X – though. Those switching from modern Macs will be a little lost at first.) The Tracker desktop combines the best aspects of Classic MacOS with the best aspects of the Windows 95 Explorer – for instance, the floating Deskbar at top right can be placed along the bottom edge of the screen, where it works perfectly as a taskbar. Menu bars are inside windows, where most people seem to prefer them, but like Classic MacOS, the contents of menus change on the fly when you hold down modifier keys. The Reg FOSS desk has been covering Haiku for some years: in 2022, when it got a port of WINE, then again at beta 4 in 2023, at beta 5 at the start of 2025, plus its new hardware 3D support later that year. It is our favorite modern x86 OS by a wide margin, even though it’s not quite ready to be our daily driver. Quite a lot of things don’t work yet. For example, there’s next to no multihead support – just a couple of ancient graphics cards can do this. However, compared to the level of fit and finish in many Linux and indeed BSD distros we’ve seen, if we were in charge of Haiku, we would have had no hesitation in calling this Version 1.0. In terms of the smoothness and completeness and coherence of its user experience, it is streets ahead of any desktop Linux that there’s ever been – or, we suspect, ever will exist. Like the Haiku devs, this vulture is not an AI user: we avoid it completely. We have seen other AI skeptics expressing concern on social media: What if the entire Linux distro world turns to AI slop, or even implodes? Where else is there to go? It is a clear and present danger: the Linux kernel team is embracing AI. So are many distros: Ubuntu is leaning in to AI tooling, then Debian voted not to limit its use, and of course Red Hat is all-in. We like to imagine a world of Haiku clients, talking to NetBSD back-end servers, and nothing but feature-phones – maybe running a revived Symbian. No AI, no Electron apps anywhere. A sky as clear and blue as the Haiku desktop, with no trace of a Cloud to be seen. That sounds idyllic to us. If it does to you as well, we think you might enjoy trying Haiku. ®

articles.title: Nvidia buys Hugging Face for $12.9B, promises not to squeeze too hard
articles.text: Nvidia has agreed to buy AI developer platform Hugging Face for $12.9 billion, tightening its grip on the ecosystem surrounding open models. Following weeks of industry chatter, Nvidia confirmed Thursday it had entered into a definitive agreement to buy the model-hosting hub, sometimes described as a GitHub for AI developers. The transaction is expected to close in the first half of 2027, subject to regulatory approval and other customary closing conditions. Open foundation models and the applications built on them drive demand for the accelerators and software Nvidia sells. Owning one of the main platforms through which developers discover and distribute those models brings the GPU giant closer to the workloads running on its hardware. Nvidia said the purchase will give Hugging Face additional resources and support developers building, sharing, and deploying open models and applications. It pledged to keep the platform open and allow model makers, developers, and users to access models and datasets of their choosing. "Open models let startups, businesses, universities and public institutions build on advanced capabilities without training every model from scratch. They enable organizations to match the right model to the right job," Nvidia chief Jensen Huang wrote in a blog announcing the move. "That is how AI can advance safely, strengthen cybersecurity and sovereignty, accelerate innovation, and reach factories, hospitals, farms, classrooms and Main Street businesses around the world." In a post on X, Hugging Face co-founder and CEO Clément Delangue said that open source AI is at an inflection point. "Thanks to the community, we've shown that it can be a complement, and even an alternative, to closed-source APIs. But for it to happen at larger scale, it needs more compute, more support, more collaboration and more visibility. That's why we went to talk to Jensen, who offered to do exactly that with us," he explained. But the move could also be seen as the industry giant further consolidating its central position in the AI industry. "Nvidia has already built an extended ecosystem through GPUs, CUDA, networking, inference software, and AI frameworks. Hugging Face will give it a stronger position at the developer, model distribution, and community layers, which will strategically help to shape where AI workloads are built and deployed," says Forrester Research principal analyst Charlie Dai. Enterprise users of Hugging Face should be alert to any shift in its open stance, he cautioned. "As Hugging Face's value comes from neutrality, Nvidia is likely to preserve openness initially. Enterprises should watch for future shifts rather than immediate disruption, while risk assessment around deeper integration with Nvidia tooling, runtimes, and optimization frameworks will be necessary over time." It will also likely renew concerns over the financial stability of the whole AI ecosystem, as a small number of very large companies and investors seem to be involved in many of the deals keeping the industry's wheels turning. Nigel Green, CEO of financial consultants deVere Group, recently compared China's AI ecosystem with America's "dangerously circular" trade. "For weeks I've been flagging that too much of the AI trade in the US is financing itself, with the same capital moving between a tight circle of suppliers, lenders and customers and getting booked as growth every time it changes hands. "A supplier invests in a customer, that customer spends the investment buying the supplier's own hardware, and the identical dollars get counted as fresh revenue at every stop along the loop," he commented. As The Register reported last month, Nvidia is increasingly using the huge profits it has made out of AI to shore up the foundations of the entire ecosystem. The GPU giant is increasingly becoming the central pillar of the AI industry, holding it all together. ®

Waldemar Geiger / Hartpunkt

The procurement project to equip the German Navy’s Sea Battalion with multi-purpose combat boats is approaching a major milestone.

According to information obtained by hartpunkt, the contract for the delivery of up to 15 such Watercat M18 AMC combat boats is expected to be awarded to the Finnish boatbuilder Marine Alutech. The system apparently prevailed in the competition against the CB90 design from the Swedish defense company Saab.

According to previous statements from the Ministry of Defence, the combat boats are intended to ensure the tactical mobility of the Sea Battalion across a wide range of missions and will be used for amphibious, military evacuation, escort, patrol and harbor protection operations.

The German Armed Forces reportedly plan to procure ten boats in a first phase and to order five more systems in the near future. Well-informed sources expect the first boats to enter service starting in 2029. Until then, the systems must undergo qualification procedures within the German Armed Forces.

The German Navy has been waiting for some time for the project to be realized, the analysis phase of which began in July 2017. However, the competitive bidding process for the procurement of 15 off-the-shelf multi-purpose boats, which are “already in service with another navy – ideally a navy of a NATO member or partner state,” was only opened in June 2023, after the possibility of financing the project from the Bundeswehr’s special fund was created in September 2022.

The Watercat M18 is a multi-purpose combat boat approximately 20 meters long with a displacement of 32 tons. The Finnish armed forces operate 12 of these systems, designated Jehu-class. Two 660 kW Scania diesel engines propel the boat to a top speed of 45 knots. Its range is approximately 200 nautical miles (370 km). The Finnish armed forces crew consists of six sailors, and the boat can also accommodate up to 25 fully equipped marines in its fighting compartment, transporting them to the shore for operations such as combat landings.

articles.title: Cybercrooks trawl Fishbrain to net password hashes
articles.text: Cybercriminals have reeled in password hashes and corresponding salts belonging to users of popular fishing app Fishbrain, opening the door to cracking attempts. Fishbrain AB, which says its eponymous app serves more than 20 million anglers, disclosed the August 19 breach to the California Attorney General's Office this week. The unknown perpetrators helped themselves to a trawl of user data, including names, dates of birth, email addresses, phone numbers, Fishbrain usernames, country information, password hashes, and salts. "Fishbrain passwords were not stored in plaintext; however, Fishbrain has determined that the compromised password hashes for some users may be susceptible to being decoded," the company said in its disclosure [PDF]. It added: "If you use your Fishbrain password for any other online accounts, you should promptly update those passwords and any associated security questions or answers. "You should also take other appropriate steps to protect any online accounts that use the same username or email address and password combination. We recommend using a strong, unique password for each of your accounts." With the hashes and salts in hand, attackers can make password guesses using their own hardware until they potentially recover the original credentials. Whether those attempts succeed depends on the strength of each password and the hashing algorithm Fishbrain used, which the company did not disclose. Fishbrain did not comment on the scale of the breach or how many of its claimed 20 million-plus users were affected. The Register asked Fishbrain for more information. After discovering the intrusion and conducting an initial forensic investigation, Fishbrain patched the vulnerability and reset every user's password. Customers must create a new one the next time they log in. Fishbrain also said it "restricted access to the affected environment," strengthened its security controls, and initiated "a broader review of our data security measures" while the investigation continues. Fisherfolk should also keep an eye out for phisherfolk using the stolen personal data to bait follow-on attacks. ®

articles.text:
India’s multiple-launch rocket system Pinaka family is set to get a major upgrade in range and capability, as Pinaka IV is apparently being developed to reach up to 300 km but tender documents reveal interesting details that the system will utilize a much bigger rocket motor of 370 mm class, as opposed to the previous Pinaka rockets.
The main benefit of a larger diameter rocket motor is that it allows to carry more propellant. For a cylindrical motor, if its length is fixed, the cross-section area will define the volume of the propellant it can carry. And the cross-section area is directly proportional to the square of its diameter, which means that the 370 mm motor will have a significantly larger cross-section area than the 214 mm motor of the previous Pinaka.
Hence, the 370 mm motor could carry roughly three times more propellant than the 214 mm one if the length of both is the same. However, it would most likely not carry three times more propellant, since the length of the motor would hardly be the same. The length of the motor would scale along with the increase in diameter in order to utilise the additional space for carrying more propellant.
Nevertheless, a larger diameter provides more room for the designer to optimise the characteristics of the motor, particularly when it comes to launching a rocket artillery system with a range of 300 km. Such a range would significantly surpass the capability of any existing or planned rocket artillery system in India, giving the Indian Army a mobile deep strike capability, rather than a purely tactical one.
Such a gun would be able to engage critical targets far behind enemy lines, including logistics nodes, command posts, air defence installations and other important infrastructure. Additionally, the larger diameter provides more space within the rocket for guidance and control systems. A guided long-range rocket system requires avionics and other equipment to navigate and control its flight path, which is best achieved with a larger diameter, while retaining the payload capacity and maintaining the required range and performance.
The rockets utilised in the Pinaka-IV system would presumably have a larger diameter than any of the existing Pinaka rockets, which have a caliber of 125 mm. Hence, the rockets would be considerably bigger and heavier than their predecessors. This will have an adverse effect on the amount of ordnance that can be carried by a single launcher, necessitating changes to storage, transportation and firing platforms. The Indian Army would have to take the opportunity to balance the range and the volume of fire, which would presumably necessitate the adoption of multiple Pinaka variants.
While the short-range rockets would provide a dense salvo of fire for engaging point targets, the larger Pinaka-IV rockets could engage more distant and important targets with more precision. The 370 mm diameter also gives the designer ample room for experimentation and future upgrades to the system. The adoption of more advanced propulsion technologies would help boost the performance of the rockets, which would most likely be decided based on the particular architecture of the Pinaka-IV, of which details are currently unknown. There is no word yet whether the system will utilise multi-pulse propulsion technology or a multi-stage design for its long-range capability.

articles.title: What a Twin-145kN Engine Class Could Mean for a 6th-Gen Fighter’s MTOW
articles.text:
There is a lot of talk about engine thrusts and numbers in defence discussions – but seldom translated to what it means for an airframe. It’s at a very interesting inflection point, in the sense that there’s now a twin-145kN configuration that’s being floated in conversations for India’s AMCA fighter and other next-generation projects. That’s more than enough power to fly a hypothetical airframe at a similar weight class like some of the heaviest fighters in use today, but which airframe it flies, depends pretty much on design philosophy, not just the power attached to it.
The afterburning ones are at 145kN each, so 2 engines together is 290kN. This figure alone is not particularly revealing. It’s all about the thrust-to-weight ratio the designer is looking for, as it essentially says what type of fighter this is supposed to be.
Reading Thrust Class Against Existing Heavy Fighters
The best method to sanity check a hypothetical airframe is to compare it to a fighter already in the air with the same combined thrust level. The F119-powered F-22 Raptor has a combined theoretical maximum take-off weight of around 38,000kg with a thrust-to-weight ratio of around 0.83. The Su-35’s twin AL-41F1S engines generate an estimated total of about 284kN, with each providing an estimated 142kN, for a 0.84 ratio for MTOW, which is near 34,500kg. The comparable AL-41F1 baseline powerplant class will place the Russian’s Su-57 between 0.85 and 0.86 at MTOW.
All these are not random occurrences. The air-superiority class fighters have been designed to be heavy and therefore have been designed to take advantage of a T/W operating range that lies somewhere between 0.8 and 0.86 at max weight, because that’s the sweet spot where they can perform a reasonable sustained turn with a decent climb rate and carry reasonable amounts of fuel or weapons.
If the same is applied to 290kN of combined thrust, the MTOW of a hypothetical twin-145kN fighter is in the range of 34,300kg and 37,000kg. This is the standard case of an airframe that is built according to known heavy-fighter design concepts and doesn’t play too much with the extremes.
Where the Estimate Moves and Why
This is where the mission philosophy is added and the range becomes significantly broader, which brings in some differences between the sixth and fifth generations. A fighter specifically designed for air superiority for instance, with a lighter internal weapons and fuel load, could get T/W into the more extreme range of approaching 1.0, which would reduce MTOW to about 29,500kg. This is a much lighter and more sleeker aircraft.
Move in the opposite direction, toward a more strike-heavy, multirole platform with an increased weapons bay for stand-off ordnance and an increased internal fuel fraction for range, and T/W declines toward 0.75, which will increase MTOW toward 39,400kg.
This is exactly what sixth generation programmes are grappling with that previous ones were not experiencing. The design of these platforms from the ground up, instead of adding on the loyal-wingman and drone-teaming structures later on, makes range and persistence more important. This is counterbalanced by the pull of MTOW but pulled down by the requirements of low observability and maneuverability. If the design of the 6th generation fighter is the air-superiority type and not the strike-heavy type (as in the 5th generation), then a realistic middle estimate of 33,000kg to 35,000kg is normal.
This means what it says: the AMCA Mk2 Conversation.
None of the above should be taken as an official specification for AMCA Mk2 or any other programme mentioned — it’s an extrapolation from physics and precedent, the type of practice that’s helpful for context, not prediction. The engines that have been in the forefront of all indigenous propulsion roadmap discussions in India have been the 110 to 130kN class for the near to medium term range and the 145kN class has been more of a long-term growth target than a baseline expectation. A twin-145kN configuration and the approximately 33-35 tonne MTOW that this entails is not a reflection of the current state of the programme but the end goal in India’s sixth generation ambitions.

articles.title: From RAM Coatings to EW: How India Could Build a Lower-Observable Su-30MKI
articles.text:
The large size of the Indian Air Force’s Su-30MKI and its traditional aerodynamics make it highly visible by radar compared to the fifth-generation fighters and make it one of the most significant platforms in the Air Force. India might not want to make the aircraft a true stealth fighter, but it could go for a more realistic approach, where it seeks to selectively decrease its radar cross-section (RCS) while simultaneously improving its electronic warfare, sensors and long-range weapons.
The most realistic and useful initial development would be radar-absorbing materials (RAM). DRDO has already developed indigenous paints and materials; including technologies based on magnetic functional fillers which are used to make radar absorbing paint. These materials may be used in various parts of the aircraft, such as the intake ducts, wing surfaces, radomes, pylons, leading edges and other sections that help to minimize radar reflections.
For the Su-30MKI, however, it just wouldn’t make a dramatic transformation to cover the whole aircraft in RAM. The geometry of the aircraft still remains the key constraint. The most efficient way would be to select and repair the areas of the airframe that scatter the greatest amount of energy caused by electromagnetic radiation, and make improvements while leaving the rest of the airframe unchanged.
An important potential one is the engine intakes. A big fighter-engine intakes can show their internal structure and lead to strong radar reflections. Some of these reflections could be minimized by selective treatment of the inlet surfaces and other surfaces that are accessible. This might be possible as part of large maintenance and overhaul cycles, but if this is to be changed it requires significant electromagnetic, structural and flight testing to prove a change.
Radar-absorbing structures and composite materials may be the next step. Fairings and panels that are not load-bearing may be able to be produced with composite construction that has a radar-absorbing property. India could start with removable panels, fairings etc and then move on to replacing the main structure of the Su-30MKI.
Other practical areas would be edges, joints and external interfaces of the aircraft. Radar scattering may be caused by leading edges, canards, intake lips, access-panel boundaries, pylons and landing-gear doors. Some of these effects can be minimized through improved alignment of the panels, through specialized properties of the surfaces, and by carefully selected radar-absorbing materials.
The canopy and radome might also be given a thorough cleaning. The electromagnetic properties of a radar transparent radome are of special significance, since it must permit the effective operation of the aircraft’s radar. Future Indian improvements may then look to find more controlled materials for the radome which would reduce unwanted reflections but not affect the performance of the radar. Likewise, a canopy that is conductive to the cockpit cavity could be an effective treatment.
Covering external weapons and fuel tanks isn’t possible, however, with any coating… The Su-30MKI is an external storage carrier and the weapons can make the plane visible to the enemy radar. It would be a major redesign of the airframe to install an internal weapons bay, and would effectively be a new aircraft rather than an upgrade.
Hence, India’s most prudent course of action would be to build a “lower-observable Su-30MKI” instead of a stealth Su-30MKI. The programme may need to be integrated with selective RAM treatment, intake improvements, radar absorbing composite panels, edge management and new technology in the area of the radome and canopy.
The survivability of the aircraft could then be enhanced by its AESA radar, its electronic warfare suite, its infrared search and track system, its passive sensors, networking and the long-range air-to-air missiles. These technologies do not reduce RCS, but they can reduce the amount of time an enemy has to detect, identify, track and engage the aircraft.
This separation becomes more significant with the advent of the long-range fight and network-centric warfare. It doesn’t have to be invisible if it can discover an enemy first, hit them with a weapon from a distance and interfere with the kill chain, as its sensors, electronic warfare, networking and weapons can do.
India might therefore move towards implementing RCS-reduction technology in the course of planned overhauls of the Su-30MKIs, rather than having to decommission significant numbers of aircraft for a major structural overhaul. This would enable the IAF to test and experiment with locally available RAM and radar absorbing structures and gather operational and test data before rolling out the changes for the entire fleet.
The goal should be simple – make the Su-30MKI harder to target and hit while maintaining its substantial range, payload and weapons load. India does not have to convert all the existing fighters to F-35. The development of truly low-observable platforms like the AMCA notwithstanding, a selectively lower-observable Su-30MKI fitted with advanced AESA (active electronically scanned array) radar, electronic warfare, passive sensors and long-range missiles could give the IAF a much more survivable heavy fighter.

articles.title: How Pakistan’s LiDAR Mapping of J&K Could Aid Future Military Operations Against India
articles.text:
If reports are true, Pakistan has been doing comprehensive LiDAR mapping of J&K which could have great impact on the military planning against India in the region. Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) technology can create very detailed 3D representations of the terrain, including elevation, slope, valley, vegetation and man-made structures, as opposed to traditional 2D maps.
The Survey of Pakistan has openly published their utilization of UAV-based LiDAR, GNSS and digital photogrammetry for high precision geospatial applications in Pakistan. But at present, there is no reliable evidence that has surfaced in the public domain of the Pakistani side of the border with Indian-administered Jammu & Kashmir to confirm the extent of J&K mapping by Pakistani LiDAR. Activity reported should therefore be considered as an allegation only in the absence of any supporting evidence.
Where they do exist, these detailed datasets would be most useful as a geospatial intelligence baseline. The geography of J&K is very complex, characterized by high mountains, narrow valleys, forests, ridgelines and a constantly evolving infrastructure. A high-resolution, 3-D terrain database could provide military planners with much more detailed knowledge of the physical battlespace than current maps.
The information may be used for terrain analysis, route assessment, line of sight and military simulation. Information on elevation can also be used with other intelligence information to determine the impact of mountains and terrain features on radar coverage, communications and surveillance.
Change detection would be an other important application. Analysts could compare the datasets to determine whether roads or other infrastructure have changed; they could also use a terrain model with older data with newer satellite or aerial imagery to determine changes in buildings and bridges. This may help to identify potential information collection needs.
LiDAR could be used in conjunction with satellite reconnaissance as well. Visual information from optical satellite imagery is detailed but may be obscured by cloud cover, shadows and vegetation. In mountainous areas and those with dense vegetation, LiDAR can provide highly accurate terrain data even in the presence of vegetation, making it valuable to these areas.
These data might be more useful if added to digital mission-planning and simulation systems. A detailed terrain database may be used to assist with terrain-referenced navigation, modelling and command and control applications. But LiDAR wouldn’t have given real-time intelligence or automatically marked military targets. If it could be integrated with other sensors and intelligence it would have military value.
In the case of artillery and air use, the availability of accurate elevation and terrain data would help modelling and planning but would require intelligence to determine the actual position and condition of the targets. Roads and bridges, military buildings and other infrastructure can undergo significant changes over time, which necessitates regular updates.
The most important benefit would then come from the integration of high resolution geospatial information and ongoing ISR capabilities. Satellite imagery, UAV reconnaissance, electronic intelligence, and other sensors would be able to update the underlying three-dimensional terrain database and would offer a much more detailed view of the operational environment.
There was already significant capability within India for geospatial intelligence and mapping of terrain. Indian agencies have been working on huge remote sensing and topographic mapping projects in the state of Jammu and Kashmir, including projects in highly undulating regions. Therefore, having access to LiDAR data in Pakistan does not necessarily mean that India is not capable of having access to it.
The meaning would then be determined by the accuracy, comprehensiveness, resolution and timeliness of the data. If Pakistan has really acquired accurate and up-to-date LiDAR data of the relevant region, it could be used as an intelligence multiplier in Pakistan’s military planning and terrain analysis processes.

articles.text:
Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever’s talks in New Delhi have delivered one significant defence-related outcome: ten agreements, including training, technology sharing, and manufacturing, were signed, among which is the 70 mm rocket assembly deal with Kalyani Strategic Systems.
The rocket assembly deal is part of the agreements concluded by De Wever during his trip to India, which also saw the participation of the Belgian Defence and Foreign Trade Minister Theo Francken and a business delegation of 15 Belgian defence firms. Under the agreement, India’s suppliers will be involved in the production process more closely than in the case of a purely Belgian assembly, with the first domestically produced rockets set to roll off the production line in early 2027. Apart from the rocket assembly, Belgium and India have signed an agreement on the production of ammunition of two calibres with equipment for two other calibres to be produced, with the annual output estimated at 100 million rounds. This contract is worth €50 million, with the deliveries due in 2028-2029. Belgium and India have also signed an agreement on naval mines and counter-mining, including drone countermeasure technologies and sensors.
What makes this announcement noteworthy is the fact that Kalyani Strategic Systems is not the first Indian rocket manufacturer to cooperate with Thales Belgium. Earlier in February 2023, Bharat Dynamics Limited (BDL) signed an MoU with Thales Belgium for the production of the FZ275 laser-guided rocket. Another Indian defence company, Adani Defence and Aerospace, has also entered the fray, signing a contract in 2024 for the production of FZ275 LGR rockets and FZ90 FFAR rockets under the Buy Indian guidelines, thus becoming a preferred supplier of ALH and LCH helicopters. By announcing Kalyani Strategic Systems as the third Indian supplier of 70 mm rockets, Thales Belgium has created competition amongst local bidders for a contract that is evidently growing in importance.
India’s requirements for 70 mm rockets are described as recurring and significant, with the weapon being integral to the combat capability of its rotary-wing aircraft, including Rudra, Prachand, and LCH helicopters. Thales itself has reportedly ramped up its production of 70 mm rockets in response to the heightened demand from NATO countries, which has been fuelled by the ongoing conflict in Ukraine. The involvement of multiple domestic suppliers in India in the production of rockets is also consistent with the trend, as it allows for a more widespread distribution of manufacturing know-how and reduces the risk associated with dependence on a sole provider for a critical defence product.
Importantly, India’s engagement in the production of 70 mm rockets appears to be beneficial to both parties, as it addresses India’s requirements for enhanced domestic manufacturing capability while also providing Thales Belgium with an alternative production base. For Belgium, the 70 mm rocket production in India is a welcome opportunity, which Thales Belgium’s CEO probably views as a way to meet the surging demand from NATO countries without further stretching the resources of its European manufacturing facilities. Indeed, Thales Belgium is the only European contractor for the production of 70 mm NATO standard rockets, and in the past two years, it has increased its production capacity five-fold in order to meet the demand.

Defence Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh, IAS, turned up at Indo-Russian Rifles Private Limited (IRRPL) for what was meant to be a routine tour of the facilities under his purview. Little did he know that this particular visit would see him first-hand witness the fruits of the indigenisation drive and also get to test-fire the rifle that IRRPL considers its crowning achievement, the “SHER”.
The Defence Secretary took a tour of IRRPL’s production and test facilities at Korwa in Amethi district, had a chat with the locals, and took a shot at the rifle that IRRPL proudly refers to as “100% Genuinely Indigenised AK-203 rifle”, the “SHER”.
IRRPL, a joint venture between India’s Defence PSU and their Russian counterparts Concern Kalashnikov and Rosoboronexport, was formed with the stated aim of manufacturing over 6 Lac AK-203 rifles indigenously as opposed to buying them from the Russians. Therefore, the completion of the indigenisation process (i.e. transitioning from imported to home-grown production of all components) is a major milestone. It was this very rifle, after recently completing the indigenisation process, that was test-fired by the Defence Secretary at the very same facility where it was produced. IRRPL claims that trials by the Indian Army are expected to commence in the coming month.
It must be noted that while the rifle previously had Indian-made components, they were procured from within the country. Now that the indigenisation process is complete, it means that each component of the rifle, including spares and accessories, is either made or sourced from within the country. The CEO of IRRPL has stated that they aim to deliver the rifles to the Indian Army a full year before the 2032 deadline mentioned in the contract, which should give us an idea about their confidence in the production and supply schedule.
Based on the accounts provided by IRRPL, the Defence Secretary’s visit was apparently the most exciting thing to have happened in the plant since its inception. While the tour of the plant and the meetings with the local workers were undoubtedly exciting for the workers, the part that captured the public’s imagination was when the Defence Secretary took a shot at the SHER rifle. In many ways, it was the most exciting thing in terms of boosting morale as a top-level authority figure taking interest in the product shows that the long hours of hard work and effort have not gone in vain. The Defence Secretary taking pot shots at the rifles was a tremendous morale booster for the workers in attendance and according to IRRPL, a “tremendous source of encouragement”.
Now that the process of indigenisation has been completed and the rifle has been officially test-fired at the Korwa plant, the next big step will be to conduct the formal trials by the Indian Army, which is expected to happen next month. This is likely to be the final step before the rifle can be declared ready for induction into the Army as per the statements made by the leadership of IRRPL. With the aforementioned contract for over 6 Lac rifles lying unfulfilled and the target delivery date being a full year earlier than what was originally envisioned, it remains to be seen if IRRPL’s optimism is warranted.

Child-monitoring apps might need a reboot

Digital harms have become the defining fear of American parents. In response, they’re increasingly turning to content-monitoring apps that scan their children’s texts, photos, emails, and chats, issuing alerts whenever an algorithm flags something it deems dangerous.

These tools have had genuine successes, preventing suicide attempts, intercepting predators, and averting school shootings. But they can also cause harm themselves, from false alarms and unnecessary interventions to damaged trust and anxiety.

Child-safety researchers say better approaches exist. Here’s what they think those could look like.

Agriculture relies on fossil fuels. It’s costing us.

Fertilizer prices have been on a roller coaster this year, driven in part by trade disruptions and high natural-gas prices. That’s because natural gas is both an energy source and a chemical input in the production of ammonia, a key fertilizer ingredient.

The war in Iran has pushed natural-gas prices higher and disrupted fertilizer trade through the Strait of Hormuz—and its closure could make access harder still for some of the world’s poorest countries.

Let’s take a closer look at the surging fertilizer prices, and how a few climate-friendly alternatives could bring farmers some relief.

'Uber rapture' leaves passengers and drivers behind in Nigeria and Uganda
articles.text: UPDATED In what some are dubbing the "Uber rapture," the ride-hailing pioneer has abruptly quit Nigeria and Uganda. Far from drivers and their cars ascending to some surge-priced afterlife, users reported the service shutting down while rides were still underway. "A friend of mine said they were on a ride when they got the message," one observer wrote on X. "She told the driver and he said, 'It's a lie!'" – a phrase widely used in Nigeria to express disbelief or call out what one perceives to be bullshit. Unfortunately for drivers who rely on the platform for their livelihood, it wasn't. The shutdown came with little apparent warning. In both countries, Uber sent notices on September 2 saying the service would cease that same day. "We are writing to share some difficult news," the email to Nigerian customers began, according to TechCabal. A separate message to drivers acknowledged: "We know this is heavy news," and promised active drivers a one-off goodwill payment "to help ease this change." Some customers lamented the service's departure, describing it as one of the country's safer transport options. Ugandan users and local partners received much the same abrupt farewell. Uber said it had been "an absolute privilege" to serve Kampala since 2016 and promised to keep in-app support available for 21 days to settle outstanding issues, according to the Daily Monitor. Rivals Faras, Bolt, and SafeBoda will now be eyeing the space it left behind. Uber confirmed that it had wound down operations in both countries on September 2. "This decision is limited strictly to these two markets and does not impact our operations across the rest of the continent," it said in a statement. "Uber remains deeply committed to sub-Saharan Africa, where we continue to see robust growth and long-term opportunity." The exits come amid a wider Uber restructuring that will cut more than 3,000 jobs, reduce management layers, and free up cash for investment in areas including autonomous vehicles, according to the BBC. Uber launched in Nigeria, Africa's most populous country, in 2014 and expanded into Uganda two years later. In Nigeria's traffic-choked commercial hub of Lagos, it even launched a boat service in 2019 to help commuters bypass the gridlock. Uber offered no explanation beyond its boilerplate about changing priorities, but Nigeria had become a tough place to make the ride-hailing sums work. Drivers had complained that fares failed to keep pace with soaring fuel costs while Uber's commissions remained stubbornly high, and the company faced growing competition from Bolt, inDrive, and local rivals, according to the BBC. The removal of Nigeria's fuel subsidy in 2023 pushed up operating costs, while inflation and another rise in petrol prices this year squeezed drivers further. Uber has not said whether those pressures prompted its exit, but they can't have made staying especially attractive. The withdrawal continues a broader retreat from Africa. Uber also left Ivory Coast and Tanzania over the past year, leaving it operating in Egypt, Ghana, Kenya, and South Africa. The Register asked Uber whether the service really ground to a halt while rides were still in progress, as reports of an "Uber rapture" suggested. We also asked when it decided to leave the two markets and how much notice it gave customers, drivers, and employees. Uber had not responded by the time of publication. Users worldwide will recognize a lesser form of rapture: a driver accepts your booking, then cancels and vanishes from the app. ® Updated at 13.15 UTC on September 3, 2026, to add: In a statement sent to The Register, an Uber spokesperson, said: "After a thorough review, we have made the difficult decision to wind down operations in Nigeria. We are deeply grateful to drivers for their dedication and contributions over the years, and we are committed to supporting them through a smooth and responsible transition. In line with global best practices, we provided a clear timeframe between communicating our decision and suspending the app, allowing drivers time to prepare. We have also been in touch with active drivers to extend a token of our appreciation and provide support during this period."

articles.title: Which came first, Windows 95's taskbar or NeXT's Dock? Neither
articles.text: Last week marked the 31st anniversary of Windows 95 going on sale. More than three decades later, suggestions about the influences behind its interface can still rile some of the people who built it. The Reg FOSS desk prompted spirited responses from several former Microsoft employees after noting possible British influences on NeXTstep and Windows 95. The exchange began with a passing comment in an X thread started by former Microsoft engineer Dave Plummer, who has spoken regularly to The Register since at least 2020. Former Microsoft executive Joe Belfiore responded: The NeXT dock did NOT lead to the taskbar.  Two things did: 1) Cairo team had been designing an always visible, bottom-of-the-screen "tray" .. which was a drop target for files, text-content, etc… to facilitate easy transfer of stuff from one place/app to another….  — Joe Belfiore (@joebelfiore) August 25, 2026 Belfiore's post has already inspired at least one article examining the taskbar's origins. The claim attracting the rebuttals comes from Paul Fellows, who led Acorn's original Arthur project. Its codename reflected the team's optimistic schedule: A Risc by THURsday. In 2022, this vulture moderated a discussion between four members of the original Acornsoft team. Organized by ROUGOL, the RISC OS User Group of London, the event marked the operating system's 35th anniversary. It was also covered by Acorn news site Icon Bar, named after the most distinctive element of Acorn's desktop. The Register subsequently published highlights from the discussion, including Fellows' views on Arthur's influence on NeXTstep and Windows. Fellows told us: "I found this page I was very pleased by: 'Apple acquired the Dock from Steve Jobs' NeXTstep OS, which stole it from Acorn's Arthur Operating System of 1987.'  "Damn right it did! Tragically, you couldn't patent software at that point. So this was the one I invented: I came up with the idea of the icon bar across the bottom. In case anyone ever asked where it came from, we were sat in a room thinking 'How do we design this to be different, so we don't get sued by Apple?' The Mac had a menu bar of text across the top, so we thought 'we can't go across the top, we'll have to go across the bottom – and we can't use text, so we'll have to use icons.' That's why it's like that." King Arthur Arthur was the original ARM OS for the first models of Acorn's new RISC-based Archimedes computers, which shipped in 1987. The Reg celebrated the Archimedes' 25th anniversary back in 2012, and that article includes a screenshot of the Arthur OS. You can see some more in the GUIdebook gallery of Arthur 1.2. Arthur's desktop was only intended to be a BASIC demo, but Acorn shipped it along with the rest of Arthur. For version 2 in 1989, Acorn gave it a slightly more technical-sounding name: RISC OS – although the design of Arthur's desktop, complete with icon bar, persisted. Fellows originally made those remarks during his first appearance at ROUGOL in 2012, for which a full transcript is available. He delivered a similar talk at the RISC OS London show in 2015, and that version is on YouTube. From a simple chronology, it looks like Acorn's Arthur had the first "icon bar" in 1987. Allegedly, a former Acorn engineer moved to California, taking his Archimedes with him, and showed it to his colleagues. The following year saw Steve Jobs unveil the NeXT Cube. ToastyTech has a screenshot gallery of NeXTstep 0.8, and you can even play with it in Infinite Mac. For historical context, Windows 2.0 was released in December 1987 with flat, outlined window controls, as GUIdebook shows. OS/2 1.1, the first version of OS/2 with its Presentation Manager GUI, followed in late 1988. Its appearance was closely related to that of Windows 2, unsurprisingly given that Microsoft and IBM had jointly developed OS/2. This OS/2 1.1 gallery shows the resemblance. NeXT demonstrated its new grayscale GUI in 1988, with pseudo-3D shading used throughout. In October 1989, IBM released OS/2 1.2, and WinWorld's images show that it had gained similar shading on window controls and dialog-box buttons. The 3D look became still more prominent in Windows 3.0, released in May 1990. The chronology and visual similarities make NeXTstep a plausible influence on the later OS/2 and Windows interfaces, although screenshots alone cannot establish that its designers copied or even consulted it. Readers can compare the images and draw their own conclusions. The Microsoft Cairo project to which Belfiore refers ran from 1991 to 1996. Development ended in the year Microsoft released Windows NT 4, whose anniversary we marked last week with a mention of Cairo. Further down Belfiore's thread, former Windows chief Steven Sinofsky posted: "The Cairo team had some NeXT machines like we did on the AFX team :)" To be clear, we are not claiming that the Windows 95 taskbar copied NeXT's dock. The two served different purposes: the original taskbar was primarily an application switcher, while the Start menu acted as the launcher. The taskbar also performed several other functions. Even so, the prior art is part of the historical record. A persistent strip along the bottom of the desktop first appeared in Acorn's Arthur, the predecessor to RISC OS, in 1987. NeXTstep had a comparable dock by 1988. By the time the Windows taskbar appeared in 1995, NeXTstep 3.3 was available for non-NeXT hardware and was well established – helped in part by the CIA buying plenty of NeXT machines, as the Wall Street Journal reported last month. ®

articles.title: Agriculture relies on fossil fuels. It’s costing us.
articles.text:
If you’ve had to fill up your vehicle’s gas tank or buy a plane ticket lately, you’ve probably felt the effects of rising fossil-fuel prices. But farmers buying fertilizer for their crops are especially aware of just how far the ripple effects of the conflict in Iran have spread.

Fertilizer prices have been on a roller coaster this year, kicked off in part by trade disruptions and high prices for natural gas, a key ingredient in fertilizer production. Let’s take a closer look at why conventional fertilizer prices are so sky-high, and how a few more climate-friendly alternatives could bring farmers some relief.

As fossil-fuel prices go up, nearly all industries are affected, since most of our economy relies on these fuels to move goods and people around.

But fertilizer is even more intertwined with these fluctuations, because natural gas is used as both an energy source and a chemical input in the production of ammonia, a key fertilizer ingredient. So as natural-gas prices have spiked in recent months because of the war in Iran, fertilizer prices have followed. (It’s worth briefly noting here that fertilizer production is also a major source of greenhouse-gas emissions, accounting for about 2% of the global total.)

Fertilizer trade is being directly affected as well, since about one-third of global seaborne trade in fertilizers passes through the Strait of Hormuz, which has been effectively closed to commercial traffic because of the conflict. Access to fertilizer could get worse for some of the poorest countries around the world because of the strait’s closure, according to a report from the World Bank. While the US largely meets demand for nitrogen fertilizers with domestic production, some imports do come from the Persian Gulf.

At one point in April, the price of urea (the most commonly applied fertilizer) climbed above $850 per metric ton. That’s 80% higher than it was before the conflict and the highest level since 2022, when the Russian invasion of Ukraine and the resulting conflict caused fertilizer costs to hit record highs. Prices have come down significantly, but forecasts remain uncertain.

“There’s just this out-of-control supply chain that’s a lot more volatile than it’s ever been,” says Travis Frey, chief technology officer of Pivot Bio, a company making fertilizer with genetically edited microbes. (For more on these microbes, how they work, and what research is still needed, check out my latest story here.) 

Pivot says its products are cost-competitive with chemical fertilizers today. And because they don’t use natural gas as an input, they aren’t subject to the same price spikes. When the war in Iran started, Pivot increased the volume it planned to produce, dropped prices, and allowed farmers to lock in prices for three years, Frey says.

That could be a major help for those farmers, because high prices could be here to stay for a while. Some fertilizer prices could remain high through at least 2028, according to a report from CoBank, one of the largest banks for the agriculture industry in the US.

That’s partly because the war has caused long-lasting damage: 31 ammonia plants in the Middle East have been affected or shut down completely. That’s on top of 20 ammonia plants that have been damaged in Russia in recent years.

Ongoing high prices can be extremely challenging for farmers. “The fertilizer price spikes, and because farmers have paper-thin margins, this is a real problem,” says Tim Schnabel, founder and CEO of Switch Bioworks, another company working on advanced microbe fertilizers.

Higher costs can help push food prices higher, causing all of us to pay more at the grocery store. (It’s not just fertilizer, by the way. Farmers are also getting hit with wild diesel prices this year.) As long as we’re relying on fertilizers made with fossil fuels, food prices will be tied up with energy prices.

Switch and Pivot are among the companies looking to make alternative fertilizers that use microbes to provide nitrogen to plants. There’s a limit to how much synthetic fertilizers these products can actually replace: Depending on the crop and conditions, Pivot says, its products can replace about 25% of synthetic fertilizer today, and the company hopes to reach 40% to 50% of the total. But these alternatives could be a start to untangling fossil fuels and food.

“We can’t keep doing it like this,” Switch’s Schnabel says. “There’s no way we can build a society where the basis of the food chain depends on fossil fuels.”

articles.title: Spurs boots VMware, cites 85% licensing saving
articles.text: Premier League football club Tottenham Hotspur has ditched VMware as part of a wider datacenter and network refresh, saving itself more than 85 percent on licensing costs - though its Chief Technology Officer says the decision wasn't purely financial. Transforming Spurs into a winning force on the pitch remains a work in progress. Off the pitch, though, the club is nearing the end of a project to overhaul the tech inside its White Hart Lane stadium in north London.  The ground holds almost 63,000 fans and runs more than 1,650 Wi-Fi access points, 840+ under seat access points, 700 Bluetooth beacons, 20,000 network access points with 1,849 IPTV screens and 519 CCTV cameras connected. A six aisle datacenter is also sited within the arena.  Rob Pickering, CTO at Spurs, told The Register that on the server, storage and networking side, the club has switched entirely to the HPE GreenLake portfolio, “underpinned by OpsRamp and Morpheus (VM Essentials).” HPE will run the hybrid cloud managed service.  In the datacenter, Spurs has moved to ProLiant Compute Gen12 servers and HPE Alletra storage MP. Connectivity is being upgraded to WiFi 7 and HPE Aruba Central with self-driving capabilities.  Why migrate from VMware? “Savings is a big part of the reason,” said Pickering. "It’s a significant amount, north of 85 percent,” less than the club was forking out for licensing.  “We moved away as we in put the infrastructure… over the last three months,” he added. “The issues with the Broadcom takeover of VMware are well known in terms of the commercial changes to their structure and the way that they engage with clients.”  Since buying VMware in 2023, Broadcom has discontinued certain standalone products in favor of bundles that are often pricier regardless of whether customers use every components. Broadcom seems only focused on VMware's 10,000 to 30,000 largest customers, out of a base that numbered 350,000 before the takeover. Pickering framed virtualization itself as a commodity: “If it's not built into a broader AI operation stack, the value is even lower again. Having that all connected back into an operation stack that our team can work from - one pane of glass - is worth more than just the saving that come from moving vendor A to vendor B. We do see significant savings from that, but really it's all part of the broader story of how do we put AI ops at the heart of what we do from a technology perspective.”  He said the tech team at Spurs is relatively small, so the "ability to use AI operations to proactively see faults and remediate them without the input of a person is really critical to us."  Spurs declined to disclose what it had been paying VMware or which VMware products it used. Pickering did, however, describe HPE VM Essentials (VME) as a "completely capable replacement." The Aruba network upgrade is “running late” and should be completed within a month. Getting it right matters as up to about 30,000 fans hop onto the stadium’s Wi-Fi at any given point during a game. The ground also doubles as a concert venue and hosts NFL matches and rugby league games too.  “The process of replacing all of those consistently in a non-impactful way - given the stadium operates really 365 days a year - is one of the hardest challenges of doing any technology project in a stadium. There's no real window of downtime in stadium.”  Of course there's the physics too: "A stadium is a giant Faraday cage. It's glass and steel. It's very hard to get RF to work. We make sure we build things that ensure the RS signal can travel the distance it needs to. We also need a lot of density to do that… We're doing like 1,800 access points across the stadium in totality. So it's significant in terms of the physical engineering challenge to get it in here, but also the radio engineering challenge."  With Spurs losing its first two Premier League Games despite spending £300 million on new players during the summer, the club’s technology upgrades may be delivering more reliable returns than its transfer business, at least for now. ®

articles.title: Scaling agentic AI pilots across the enterprise
articles.text:
As agentic AI moves from experimentation toward enterprise deployment, the challenge is figuring out how agents can work together, connect to the systems and data they need, and operate safely across the workflows that run a business. Although agentic AI has been adopted by some 80% of Fortune 500 companies, progress toward meaningful scale remains uneven, with many organizations still working through isolated pilots.

WATCH THE WEBCAST

For Arun Chandra, chief operating officer at NiCE, the first step is moving beyond experimentation for its own sake. “Everybody’s trying to figure out what can we do with this technology?” he says. But scaling requires a clearer connection to business strategy: Organizations need to define whether they are trying to increase revenue, reduce costs, or pursue another strategic or financial objective. From there, they need to rethink the workflows where agents will operate instead of just layering AI onto existing processes. “The last thing you want to do is to apply AI on an outdated or an inefficient workflow,” Chandra says.

That shift requires organizations to treat agentic AI as a cohesive system. Agents need access to the data, knowledge, and context required to make effective decisions, as well as connections to back-end systems if they are expected to take action. Fragmented information can undermine those capabilities: “The efficacy of these AI agents is purely a function of the context, the knowledge, and the data they can ingest and use,” Chandra says.

The organizational implications are equally noteworthy. Scaling agents can create a new form of fragmentation if teams build isolated systems that don’t connect with one another, while governance, privacy, security, and change management become more important as agents take on more consequential work. Chandra argues that AI agents should ultimately be held to the same standards as human workers, with organizations thinking of their workforce as a combination of humans and AI agents.

Looking ahead, that connected approach could enable agents to work proactively and even communicate with other agents to resolve customer needs. For organizations making the transition from pilots to scale, the priority is not to “boil the ocean,” Chandra says, but to instead build a connected strategy around high-value use cases, workflows, workforce changes, and measurable outcomes.

articles.title: UK's Online Safety Act has made 'absolutely no difference,' kids say
articles.text: Children have told England's Children's Commissioner, Dame Rachel de Souza, that the UK's Online Safety Act (OSA) "has made absolutely no difference" to their ability to access harmful content online. More than a year after the OSA's key child protection duties took effect, de Souza told MPs and peers that young people had little understanding of the legislation or how it was intended to change their online experiences. De Souza made the comments during the opening evidence session of the House of Lords Communications and Digital Committee's inquiry into the OSA's implementation and impact. Central to de Souza's criticism was the legislation's focus on moderating harmful content rather than addressing potentially harmful platform design features. UK politicians had pushed for controls covering such features, either through the OSA or separate legislation, but none has materialized. De Souza said she was "really cross" that there was no hard evidence showing the OSA had meaningfully changed how social media platforms operate. She contrasted that with the US, where legal pressure recently pushed Meta toward significant child safety concessions. Concerns about addictive platform design are not new, but they have returned to prominence following Meta's proposed $18 billion settlement in a US child safety case. Without admitting wrongdoing, Zuckercorp would under the proposed settlement introduce two-hour daily limits for users under 18 on Facebook and Instagram, prompts intended to discourage endless scrolling, and measures addressing use during school hours and at night. The proposal would also let children opt out of algorithmically ranked feeds, directly addressing concerns raised by de Souza and other UK lawmakers. Discussing the proposed Meta settlement, de Souza said the OSA had "not been flexible enough" and had not "kept up with the time." She argued that Ofcom and lawmakers should seek results comparable to those achieved through the US legal system, even if that required the legislation to evolve. 'Furious' with Ofcom De Souza said she planned to exercise her statutory powers to compel Ofcom, the OSA's regulator, to provide copies of the safety risk assessments submitted by technology companies. The commissioner said Ofcom had refused to share the assessments with her, despite her position as "the most senior safeguarding person in this country for children," and had indicated that it would resist disclosure even if she invoked those powers. "One thing I did want to ask this committee was for your assistance in this matter, because I am planning to use my powers," De Souza said. "If we cannot even see the risk assessments that may well have put these [safety] mechanisms into place, or may not have, how on earth can we judge the efficacy of it? "So I'll leave that one with you, but I'm pretty furious about that." The obstacle is section 393(1) of the Communications Act 2003, which restricts Ofcom's disclosure of information obtained through its regulatory functions. Ofcom may disclose such information if the business concerned consents or if one of the statutory gateways in section 393(2) applies. Asked whether compelling tech companies to complete risk assessments was enough to ensure meaningful change or whether further legislation was needed, the Children's Commissioner said "we need a few things," including for Ofcom to "use its teeth." Ofcom has materially upped its presence in the tech regulation landscape during the past year, stepping in on multiple occasions when needed. Perhaps most notably this was at the height of the Grok nudifying furore, but also its sprawling list of investigations into pornography companies allegedly violating age verification requirements. De Souza acknowledged all of this, and the fact that since the introduction of the latest US administration, UK politicians have not given the regulator the "air cover" needed to relentlessly pursue offenders. Nevertheless, she said Ofcom had failed to bare its teeth as forcefully as the current technology landscape demanded and accused it of reacting to harms rather than anticipating them. "If Ofcom is going to be the vehicle to protect our children… we need them to be getting ahead of the harms. And I don't think they have. "So when I talk around the country to children, what's worrying them are things around AI, things around the nudifying apps… there are new harms, and we need Ofcom to be getting ahead of those. I don't think they are." De Souza called on UK politicians "to be really strong and direct" in empowering Ofcom to pursue offending organizations. "But how effective do I think they've been? Not effective enough." The commissioner also criticized Ofcom's child safety codes under the OSA, which she said read more like technical documents for technology companies than protections designed for children. She also called on Ofcom to "use all their powers," impose "some big fines," and act before new harms become entrenched. The Register asked Ofcom to respond. A spokesperson said: "We work closely with the Children's Commissioner and share her objectives to ensure children are safe online. "In December, we published our analysis of risk assessments from the first year of the Online Safety Act being in force, and the improvements we expected to see from platforms. "Our action has resulted in material improvements being made to risk assessments, ensuring that tech companies must implement all measures necessary to address the risks identified on their sites and apps. "We are subject to laws that mean we're restricted in what information we can disclose relating to businesses." ®
articles.summary: Children have told England's Children's Commissioner, Dame Rachel de Souza, that the UK's Online Safety Act (OSA) "has made absolutely no difference" to their ability to access harmful content online.

articles.title: British wind power to drive Maersk container ship
articles.text: Shipping giant Maersk is testing a modern rotor sail from British firm Anemoi Marine Technologies in an effort to cut fuel consumption and greenhouse gas emissions. Anemoi says Maersk will fit one of its rotor sail systems to an 8,700 TEU Lima-class container ship. TEU, or twenty-foot equivalent unit, is the standard measure of container-carrying capacity. That makes the Lima-class vessels relative tiddlers in the container-shipping world. Rival MSC's Irina-class ships measure 400 m (1,312 feet) long and can carry 24,346 TEU. Under the agreement, Anemoi will design and manufacture a rotor sail measuring 5 m (16 feet) in diameter and 35 m (115 feet) high. Promotional images identify the vessel as the Maersk Labrea. Anemoi will provide the engineering and installation support needed to integrate the sail with the ship's existing systems. Installation is scheduled for mid-2027, after which it will be tested during regular voyages across the North and South Atlantic. Rotor sails, also known as Flettner rotors, differ radically in appearance and operation from traditional sails. They use the Magnus effect, in which a spinning body moving through an airstream generates lift. The rotor's surface moves with the airflow on one side and against it on the other, creating a pressure difference and a force perpendicular to the apparent wind. When that force has a component in the ship's direction of travel, it provides additional thrust and reduces the load on the engines. Anemoi claims that a ship equipped with three of its rotor sails achieved average net fuel and emissions savings of 9.1 percent during a year-long assessment, rising to 21 percent on some voyages. "We're delighted to be working with Maersk on this pioneering project. It's a strong example of how collaboration can support the adoption of wind-assisted propulsion, and we look forward to carrying out the installation and working together as the project progresses," said CEO Clare Urmston. Maersk head of fleet technology Ole Graa Jakobsen commented: "Wind-assisted propulsion is one of several promising maritime solutions with the potential to improve vessel efficiency and reduce emissions. It has already been tested in other parts of the shipping sector, and we see this pilot with Anemoi as a valuable opportunity to build practical experience and assess its relevance for our fleet and for container shipping more broadly." The trial comes as the International Maritime Organization (IMO) pushes the shipping industry to reduce total annual greenhouse gas emissions by at least 20 percent from 2008 levels by 2030 and at least 70 percent by 2040, before reaching net zero by or around 2050. ®

articles.title: Terminated employee cost company hundreds of thousands of dollars because nobody revoked access
articles.text: PWNED Welcome back to PWNED, where we talk about organizations that are independently self-owned. This week’s tale of toxic tech involves a disgruntled ex-employee who had the means and opportunity to wreak havoc. Our story comes courtesy of Yad Senapathy, who serves as CEO of the Project Management Training Institute in Dallas, Texas. He recalls a time many years ago when he used to work in IT at a company with more than 1,000 employees. While Senapathy was working there, the company terminated an employee, but nobody cut off his access to internal systems. The angry worker logged back in, then deleted files, locked out other people's accounts, and even corrupted a database. "Several days passed where the person was no longer on payroll, but their credentials were still active," Senapathy said. "Nobody had been clearly assigned to shut them off. HR thought IT would handle it once the termination was processed. IT was waiting for HR to send a formal request. I've learned that when nobody is clearly responsible and there is no set deadline, these things can easily get missed until there is already a problem." This lapse in responsibility meant the terminated employee had access to shared admin credentials, account controls, and project tracking systems. Each of these, in turn, granted permission to other systems, leading to a domino effect of inappropriate access, which the former worker used to wreak revenge on the whole organization. According to Senapathy, the damage amounted to hundreds of thousands of dollars. Just as bad were the weeks of delay added to an important project. As an added irony, recovery was particularly difficult because the systems were damaged by the very person who best knew how to repair them. “The employee wasn't some genius hacker. They just still had access after they left and nobody changed the credentials or reviewed admin rights,” Senapathy told The Register. “We'd let one person collect so much system knowledge that shutting the door behind them took longer than it should have.” Senapathy recommends that offboarding checklists and access reviews should be right next to “return the laptop” on that list. The problem in this case is that the terminated employee had more access than most people, and so IT didn't know what they needed to cut off. “Sadly, it could've been prevented by same-day deletion of access, forced re-review of shared account access and zero tolerance for one person owning a whole system alone,” he said. This writer can identify with this situation. At a previous job, after I quit, I lost email, chat, and shared drive access, but months later my former boss asked if I could still log into an important database that was hosted externally and show him how to use it. I had no problems getting in. Have a story about someone leaving a gaping hole in their network? Share it with us at pwned@sitpub.com. Anonymity is available upon request.®
